cards.title: Kermer and colleagues · expected and actual emotions after a coin flip
cards.aim: Do people predict their emotions after a win or a loss accurately?
cards.manipulated: Outcome of a coin flip: win an extra $5 or lose $3 (after being given $5). Predicted feelings (before the flip) were compared with actual feelings (after).
cards.measured: Happiness ratings: a baseline rating before the experiment, then predicted and actual changes from baseline.
cards.found: Before the flip, people expected losing $3 to drop happiness about 4 points and winning $5 to raise it about 2 points. After the flip, the real drop was about 1 point and the real rise about 1.2 points.
cards.means: People overestimate how bad a loss will feel, because they ignore their coping mechanisms; this feeds risk aversion.
cards.trap: The loss was the smaller amount of money ($3 vs $5) but was expected to hurt about twice as much as the gain helped.

cards.title: Simonsohn · cloudy days, admissions, and enrollment
cards.aim: Does the weather, an incidental factor, carry into important decisions?
cards.manipulated: Weather: cloudy vs sunny days (on the day of the admissions decision, or the day of the campus visit).
cards.measured: Admissions decisions (what was weighted) and whether visiting students enrolled.
cards.found: Simonsohn (2007): applicants' academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days than sunny days. Simonsohn (2009): visitors to a highly rated university were more likely to enroll if they visited on a cloudy day.
cards.means: Weather is an incidental factor that can change important decisions even though it is unrelated to the applicant or the school.
cards.trap: Do not mix up the two years: 2007 is admissions decisions, 2009 is enrollment by visitors.

cards.title: Lerner and colleagues · mood and highlighter prices
cards.aim: Can a mood unrelated to the decision change how much an object seems worth?
cards.manipulated: Film clip watched first: sad (a person dying), disgust (a person using a dirty toilet), or neutral (fish at the Great Barrier Reef).
cards.measured: Selling price and buying price for a set of highlighters.
cards.found: Selling: neutral about $4.50, disgust about $2.70, sad about $3.00. Buying: neutral about $3.50, disgust about $3.00, sad about $4.50.
cards.means: Incidental mood influences decisions: disgust lowered both prices, and sadness lowered selling but raised buying.
cards.trap: Sad lowers the selling price but RAISES the buying price; disgust lowers both.

cards.title: Physicians · earlier cases and cesarean recommendations
cards.aim: Does the context of earlier cases change a decision about the same case?
cards.manipulated: What came before the same test case: nothing (control), four serious-complication cases, or four fairly routine (not serious) cases.
cards.measured: Whether physicians recommended a cesarean section for the test case.
cards.found: Significantly more doctors recommended cesarean after reading the non-serious cases first.
cards.means: Context, including recently considered cases, changes how the same patient is judged.
cards.trap: The test case never changed; only the cases before it did.

cards.title: Organ donation · opt-in and opt-out consent
cards.aim: Does the way the choice is presented change how many people become organ donors?
cards.manipulated: Opt-in procedure (must take a step to be a donor) vs opt-out procedure (a donor unless you ask not to be).
cards.measured: Consent rate in countries using each procedure.
cards.found: Opt-in countries have under 28% consent; opt-out countries have over 99% consent.
cards.means: The status quo bias, the tendency to do nothing when a decision is difficult, makes the default decide the result.
cards.trap: Doing nothing means non-donor under opt-in but donor under opt-out.

cards.title: Tversky and Kahneman · the disease problem in gain and loss frames
cards.aim: Does describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses change risk-taking?
cards.manipulated: Frame: gain frame (A: 200 saved for certain; B: 1/3 chance all 600 saved, 2/3 chance none) vs loss frame (C: 400 die for certain; D: 1/3 chance no one dies, 2/3 chance all 600 die).
cards.found: Gain frame: 72% chose A (sure), 28% chose B. Loss frame: 78% chose D (gamble), 22% chose C.
cards.means: The framing effect: gains push people to risk aversion (sure thing), losses push them to risk taking (gamble), though A=C and B=D.
cards.trap: A and C are the same outcome, and B and D are the same gamble; only the wording changed.

cards.title: Sanfey and colleagues · the ultimatum game and the anterior insula
cards.aim: Do emotion and brain activity explain why people reject unfair offers that cost them money?
cards.manipulated: Offer size ($5/$5, $7/$3, $8/$2, $9/$1) and partner type (human vs computer); each participant played 20 games, 10 with each partner type.
cards.measured: Whether the responder accepted or rejected, plus activation of the right anterior insula.
cards.found: $5/$5 and $7/$3 were accepted almost always. $8/$2 was accepted about 53% (human) vs 85% (computer); $9/$1 about 37% (human) vs 68% (computer). More right anterior insula activation meant rejecting more offers.
cards.means: Emotion (anger at unfairness) is important in decision making; utility theory says accept any offer, but people do not.
cards.trap: Utility theory says accept any offer because any money beats nothing; rejecting costs both players.

cards.title: Belief bias · judging invalid believable conclusions
cards.aim: Does a believable conclusion make people accept a syllogism as valid?
cards.measured: Whether participants judged the syllogism valid.
cards.found: 71% judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid.
cards.means: Belief bias: people judge by whether the conclusion sounds true instead of whether it follows.
cards.trap: Example: All of the students are tired / Some tired people are irritable / Some of the students are irritable sounds fine but is not valid.

cards.title: Conditional syllogisms · four forms and accuracy
cards.aim: Which kinds of if-then syllogisms do people judge correctly?
cards.manipulated: The four forms, all with If p, then q: p (modus ponens), not q (modus tollens), q, and not p.
cards.measured: Whether participants judged each form valid or invalid correctly.
cards.found: Modus ponens (valid) 97% correct; modus tollens (valid) 60%; syllogism 3 (invalid) 40%; syllogism 4 (invalid) 40%.
cards.means: Both valid forms were judged correctly more often than both invalid ones, but modus tollens is much harder than modus ponens even though both are valid.
cards.trap: Modus tollens is valid; syllogisms 3 and 4 are not.

cards.title: Wason four-card problem · abstract and concrete versions
cards.aim: Does using real-world items make conditional reasoning easier?
cards.manipulated: Abstract version (cards E, K, 4, 7; rule: vowel then even number) vs concrete version (cards Beer, Soda, 16 years old, 21 years old; rule: drinking beer then 21 years old).
cards.measured: Which cards participants chose to turn over.
cards.found: Abstract: 46% chose 4 (error), only 7% chose 7 (correct). Concrete: 73% answered correctly.
cards.means: Following the falsification principle, look for cases that break the rule; permission schemas in familiar rules make this easier.
cards.trap: Correct cards are E and 7 (abstract) and beer and 16 years old (concrete); the 4 and the 21 cannot break the rule.

contrasts.title: Valid vs true

a.definition: The conclusion follows logically from the two premises; depends on the form of the reasoning.

contrasts.tell: Ask two separate questions: does it follow? and are the statements correct? A valid syllogism with a false premise can have a false conclusion.
contrasts.example: All birds are animals / All animals have four legs / All birds have four legs is valid but its conclusion is false because premise 2 is false.

contrasts.title: Modus ponens vs modus tollens

a.definition: If p, then q; p; therefore q. Valid; 97% correct.

b.definition: If p, then q; not q; therefore not p. Valid; 60% correct.

contrasts.tell: Ponens affirms p and gets q. Tollens denies q and gets not p. Both are valid; tollens just feels harder.
contrasts.example: If I study, I'll get a good grade; I didn't get a good grade; therefore I didn't study.

contrasts.title: Modus tollens vs syllogism 3 (q, therefore p)

a.definition: Second premise is not q; conclusion not p. Valid.

b.definition: Second premise is q; conclusion p. Not valid.

contrasts.tell: Valid forms move from p to q or from not q to not p. Going from q back to p is not valid because there may be other ways to get q.
contrasts.example: If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona; I live in Arizona; therefore I live in Tucson does not follow.

contrasts.title: Syllogism 3 vs syllogism 4

a.definition: If p then q; q; therefore p. Not valid; 40% correct.

b.definition: If p then q; not p; therefore not q. Not valid; 40% correct.

contrasts.tell: Both are invalid. In 3 the second premise is q; in 4 it is not p.
contrasts.example: Syllogism 4: If I study, I'll get a good grade; I didn't study; therefore I didn't get a good grade (a good grade could come another way).

contrasts.title: Deductive reasoning vs belief bias

a.definition: Determining whether a conclusion logically follows from premises.

b.definition: Thinking a syllogism is valid because its conclusion is believable.

contrasts.tell: Deduction asks if the conclusion follows. Belief bias answers by asking if the conclusion sounds true.
contrasts.example: 71% judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid.

contrasts.title: Abstract vs concrete Wason problem

a.definition: Cards E, K, 4, 7 with the rule vowel then even number; correct cards E and 7.

b.definition: Cards Beer, Soda, 16 years old, 21 years old with the rule drinking beer then 21 years old; correct cards beer and 16.

contrasts.tell: Same if p, then q form. Concrete, familiar content calls up a permission schema and correct answers jump (73% answered the beer version correctly; only 7% chose the 7 in the abstract version).
contrasts.example: 7% chose the 7 in the abstract version; 73% answered the beer version correctly.

contrasts.title: Mental models vs belief bias

a.definition: Build a model of the premises, make a tentative conclusion, search for exceptions, then decide validity.

b.definition: The tendency to think a syllogism is valid if its conclusion is believable.

contrasts.tell: The mental model approach decides validity by searching for an exception; belief bias decides by whether the conclusion sounds believable.
contrasts.example: A conclusion is valid only if no model of the premises refutes it.

contrasts.title: Gain frame vs loss frame

a.definition: Outcomes stated as people saved; people prefer the sure option (risk aversion).

b.definition: Outcomes stated as people who die; people prefer the gamble (risk taking).

contrasts.tell: Same facts, different wording. Gains lead to the sure thing, losses lead to the gamble.
contrasts.example: 72% chose sure Program A; 78% chose gamble Program D.

contrasts.title: Opt-in vs opt-out

a.definition: You must take a step to be a donor; under 28% consent.

b.definition: You are a donor unless you request not to be; over 99% consent.

contrasts.tell: Look at what doing nothing gives you. Status quo bias: many people do nothing.
contrasts.example: Doing nothing leaves you a non-donor under opt-in and a donor under opt-out.

contrasts.title: Expected emotions vs incidental emotions

a.definition: Emotions people predict they will feel about an outcome.

b.definition: Emotions not specifically related to the decision (disposition, recent experience, surroundings).

contrasts.tell: Expected emotions are predictions about the outcome itself. Incidental emotions come from something unrelated.
contrasts.example: Kermer: predicted feelings about a coin flip. Lerner: mood from a film clip.

explainers.title: What a syllogism is and its parts
explainers.plain: A syllogism is the basic form of deductive reasoning, introduced by Aristotle. It has two premises and a conclusion.
steps: 1. Find the two premises: the statements the reasoning starts from.
2. Find the conclusion: the third statement, what you arrive at.
3. Ask only one thing: does the conclusion follow from the two premises?
explainers.example: Premise 1: All birds are animals. Premise 2: All animals eat food. Conclusion: Therefore, all birds eat food. Birds are inside animals, animals are inside things that eat food, so birds are inside that group too.
explainers.watchOut: A categorical syllogism uses all, no, or some about two categories. Do not mix it up with the conditional syllogism, which starts with If p, then q.

explainers.title: How to check validity, step by step
explainers.plain: There is no easy method, so picture the situation the premises describe and try to break the conclusion (the mental model approach).
steps: 1. Build a picture (model) of the situation the two premises describe.
2. Write a tentative conclusion, one that might hold.
3. Look for an exception: a case where the premises are true but the conclusion is not.
4. If you find one exception, the syllogism is not valid. If no model of the premises refutes the conclusion, it is valid.
explainers.example: All of the students are tired; Some tired people are irritable; so Some of the students are irritable. Everything sounds reasonable, but the conclusion does not follow from the premises, so the syllogism is not valid.
explainers.watchOut: Do not stop at the first model that fits. A conclusion is valid only if NO model of the premises refutes it.

explainers.title: Validity versus truth
explainers.plain: Valid means the conclusion follows from the premises. True means the statement matches the world. They are different.
steps: 1. Ignore whether the statements sound true.
2. Check only the form: does the conclusion follow from the two premises?
3. Then separately ask whether each statement is actually true.
4. Remember: valid plus true premises forces a true conclusion; valid with a false premise can give a false conclusion.
explainers.example: All birds are animals; All animals have four legs; All birds have four legs. It has the same form as the first example, so it is valid. The conclusion is false only because premise 2 is false.
explainers.watchOut: A syllogism can be invalid even if every statement and the conclusion seem reasonable (the students example). Valid does not guarantee a true conclusion.

explainers.title: Belief bias
explainers.plain: Belief bias is thinking a syllogism is valid just because its conclusion is believable.
steps: 1. Notice if your gut says the conclusion is true.
2. Set that feeling aside.
3. Check whether the conclusion follows from the premises (look for an exception).
4. Judge validity from that, not from belief.
explainers.example: 71% of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid. All of the students are tired; Some tired people are irritable; Some of the students are irritable sounds right but is not valid.
explainers.watchOut: Good reasoning and truth are not the same thing; do not accept reasoning just because the ending sounds true.

explainers.title: Conditional syllogisms: the four forms cheat sheet
explainers.plain: All four start with If p, then q. p is the condition and q is what follows. They differ in the second premise.
steps: 1. Write the first premise as If p, then q.
2. Identify the second premise: p, not q, q, or not p.
3. Match it: p so q (valid); not q so not p (valid); q so p (not valid); not p so not q (not valid).
4. Valid forms: go forward from p, or backward from not q.
explainers.example: If I study, I'll get a good grade. Form 1: I studied, so I'll get a good grade (97% correct). Form 2: I didn't get a good grade, so I didn't study (60%). Form 3: I got a good grade, so I studied (40%). Form 4: I didn't study, so I didn't get a good grade (40%).
explainers.watchOut: Two are valid and two are not. Both valid types were judged correctly more often than both invalid ones.

explainers.title: Modus ponens and modus tollens (the valid ones)
explainers.plain: Modus ponens: the condition is met, so the result follows. Modus tollens: the result did not happen, so the condition did not happen.
steps: 1. Modus ponens: If p, then q; p; therefore q.
2. Modus tollens: If p, then q; not q; therefore not p.
3. Test tollens in words: if studying always leads to a good grade, no good grade means no studying.
4. Both are valid with any content.
explainers.example: If I study, I'll get a good grade. I didn't get a good grade. Therefore, I didn't study. Valid, though only 60% judged it correctly (vs 97% for modus ponens).
explainers.watchOut: Modus tollens is just as valid as modus ponens, yet people find it much harder.

explainers.title: Why syllogisms 3 and 4 are not valid
explainers.plain: If p, then q says what happens when p is true. It does not say q happens only then, and it says nothing about when p is false.
steps: 1. Syllogism 3 (q so p): the premise does not say studying is the only way to get a good grade.
2. Swap in other content to test it: If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona; I live in Arizona; so I live in Tucson fails.
3. Syllogism 4 (not p so not q): the premise says nothing about not studying, and a good grade could come another way.
4. If you can find a case where the premises hold but the conclusion fails, it is not valid.
explainers.example: Syllogism 4: If I study, I'll get a good grade; I didn't study; therefore I didn't get a good grade. A person could get a good grade for some other reason, so the conclusion does not follow.
explainers.watchOut: Only 40% got each of these right. The first premise does not support either conclusion.

explainers.title: Mental models (Johnson-Laird, 1999) and the pool table
explainers.plain: A mental model is a specific situation pictured in your mind that you use to judge a syllogism.
steps: 1. Create a model of the situation.
2. Generate tentative conclusions about the model.
3. Look for exceptions that falsify the model.
4. Decide validity from whether an exception exists.
explainers.example: Pool table: a black ball directly above the cue ball, the green ball on the right of the cue ball, a red ball between them. The slide's answer is that the cue ball is to the left of the line of sight. Most people solve it by imagining the arrangement.
explainers.watchOut: One model that fits the premises but not the conclusion is enough to reject the conclusion.

explainers.title: The Wason four-card problem (abstract)
explainers.plain: To test a rule, look for cards that could break it. This is the falsification principle.
steps: 1. Rule: if there is a vowel on one side, then there is an even number on the other.
2. Ask for each card: could its hidden side break the rule?

3. E: a non-even number behind it would break the rule, so turn it. K: not a vowel, cannot break it. 4: cannot break the rule whatever is behind it. 7: a vowel behind it would break the rule, so turn it.
4. Answer: turn E and 7.
explainers.example: Cards E, K, 4, 7. 46% wrongly chose 4; only 7% chose the correct 7.
explainers.watchOut: The 4 feels right because it fits the rule, but it cannot break the rule; most people fail to look for falsifying cases.

explainers.title: Concrete Wason version and permission schemas
explainers.plain: A permission schema is the idea that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. Familiar rules like a drinking age call it up and make the problem easier.
steps: 1. Rule: If drinking beer, then 21 years old.
2. Find the case that breaks it: someone drinking beer who is under 21.
3. Turn over beer (check the age) and 16 years old (check the drink).
4. Soda and 21 years old cannot break the rule.
explainers.example: Cards Beer, Soda, 16 years old, 21 years old. 73% answered correctly. Being 21 is the condition; drinking beer is what can then be done.
explainers.watchOut: The form is the same as the vowel rule. Familiarity is not always important, so the improvement does not come from familiarity alone; context that calls up a permission schema matters.

explainers.title: Framing effect: gain versus loss
explainers.plain: The same facts worded as gains or as losses change what people choose.
steps: 1. Gain frame (saved): sure option vs gamble; people avoid risk.
2. Loss frame (die): sure option vs gamble; people take the risk.
3. Check that A equals C (200 saved = 400 die) and B equals D (same gamble).
4. Conclude that only the wording changed.
explainers.example: 600 people at risk. A: 200 saved for certain (72% chose it); B: 1/3 chance all saved, 2/3 none. C: 400 die for certain (22%); D: 1/3 nobody dies, 2/3 all die (78%).
explainers.watchOut: It is a switch in strategy caused by wording alone, not a difference in the outcomes.

notes: No researcher is named on the slides for the physician cesarean study, the organ donation rates, belief bias, the conditional syllogism percentages or the Wason problem, so none was added.
The slides do not explain why the cue ball is 'to the left' in the pool table problem beyond a brief description; the card repeats the slide's answer without adding detail.

The slides say there is no easy method for judging validity and then present mental models as one approach; the explainers follow that. They do not teach formal methods (such as diagrams) that the slides do not mention.
Slide 20 names the mental model approach as Johnson-Laird (1999); the slides give no researcher for the Wason problem, so none is attached.
